userJob: Decide whether plain HTML and CSS is enough for this build
problem: A build step, a framework and a component library are added by habit, so a page that needed two files arrives with a dependency tree someone has to maintain
worksWhen: No stack was detected, or the brief is a small number of pages with no application behaviour
avoidWhen: The project already has a stack, where its conventions govern and this does not apply
mechanism: Four conditions make a stack sufficient: something renders HTML, styles are authored in one system, there is a way to serve the pages while you work, and there is an output you can copy to a host. Here the first two are the files themselves and the last two are a local static server and the directory. Do not add beyond this without being asked. If CSS can do it, use CSS. Serve the scaffold and open it before writing any design code, so a stack failure arrives as one rather than as a design failure later.
risks: Adding a build step for one convenience, which then owns the project's deployment
Discovering the serving setup is broken after the design is built, so the two failures arrive together
mobileRules: Open the served scaffold at 375px as part of the first check, not only at desktop
accessibilityRules: A no-build project has no framework defaults to inherit, which means every semantic element is an explicit choice
genericnessNote: A sufficiency test constrains dependencies rather than appearance.

userJob: Respond correctly when the brief names a design system or an aesthetic
problem: A named design system gets approximated by hand and a named aesthetic gets an invented package, so one loses the system's real behaviour and the other claims something that does not exist
worksWhen: The brief names either a real design system or a visual style
avoidWhen: The brief names neither, where this is not a decision that has to be made
mechanism: If the brief names a real design system, install the official package and use its own components rather than approximating one, and never mix two in one project. Confirm the package name and current version against the registry at build time rather than trusting a name written down anywhere. If the brief names an aesthetic instead, there is no package to install and none to claim: build it natively.
risks: Approximating a system by hand, which loses its behaviour and keeps only its appearance
Installing a package whose name resembles the aesthetic, which is a claim about provenance
mobileRules: An installed system brings its own responsive behaviour; check it against the brief rather than assuming it matches
accessibilityRules: An official system's components usually carry accessibility behaviour a hand approximation does not, which is the main reason to install rather than approximate
genericnessNote: An installed system at its defaults is the vendor's design, so the restyle from the direction's own tokens is what makes it this client's page.

userJob: Diagnose a CSS rule that reads correctly and does nothing
problem: You are writing the cascade by hand, so two selectors of comparable weight against the same element cancel each other out, and the symptom is a rule that looks right in the file
worksWhen: Any no-build CSS project past a few hundred lines
avoidWhen: A project with scoped styles or utility classes, where the failure mode is different
mechanism: Keep one class per concern so selector weight stays flat. When a value does not take, read the computed style in the browser rather than re-reading the stylesheet, because the file cannot show you which rule won.
risks: Raising specificity to win, which sets the new floor for every later rule
Reaching for the important flag, which removes the cascade as a tool for the rest of the project
mobileRules: Specificity conflicts frequently surface only inside a media query, so read the computed style at the width where the symptom appears
accessibilityRules: Focus indicators are commonly the casualty, because they are declared once and overridden by a later broader rule

userJob: Handle a component source or asset API that requires an account
problem: Setup reaches for a service that needs a key, so the build either stalls or the key ends up written into a config file on the user's behalf
worksWhen: Any setup step that would require an account, a key or a paid plan
avoidWhen: The user has already provided the credential themselves and asked for it to be used
mechanism: Name the service as an option and let the user decide. Do not ask for, store, or write API keys into config on the user's behalf. If the option is declined, say what the build does instead rather than silently substituting something.
risks: A key written into a file that later gets committed
Substituting a different service without saying so, which changes the project's dependencies invisibly

userJob: Judge whether a hand-built page has become overloaded
problem: With no component system enforcing structure, controls and links accumulate freely, and the page's density is judged by the person who has watched it grow
worksWhen: Any decision point on a hand-built page: navigation, a filter row, a set of same-weight controls
avoidWhen: A deliberately dense reference page, where the count is the content
mechanism: At any decision point, count the visible interactive options, the top-level navigation entries, and the competing same-weight elements. Four or fewer is manageable, five to seven is the boundary, eight or more is overloaded. Counting replaces judgement, which is what makes the check survive familiarity with the page.
risks: Reducing the count by hiding options behind a control, which moves the problem
Counting only buttons and missing same-weight links and cards
mobileRules: Count against the 375px view, where collapsed navigation changes what competes with what
accessibilityRules: Options moved behind a disclosure stay reachable by keyboard and announce their expanded state
genericnessNote: A measurement produces different answers for different content.

userJob: Use a snippet, generated block or vendored component in a no-build project
problem: Vendored markup is pasted in with its own styles attached, so one section of the page belongs to a different design system and the direction breaks exactly there
worksWhen: Any build that pastes in an external snippet, a generated block or a copied component
avoidWhen: The brief asked for that system's own appearance by name
mechanism: Restyle anything generated or vendored from the direction's own token layer before it ships, because at default styling it is the vendor's design and it is the same design on every site that installed it. In a no-build project that means rewriting its classes against your own, not appending an override stylesheet after it.
risks: Appending overrides rather than replacing, which leaves two systems and a specificity war
Keeping the vendored markup structure when only the appearance was needed
mobileRules: Vendored snippets often carry their own breakpoints, which will not match yours; check 375px and 768px after restyling
accessibilityRules: Vendored markup can carry roles and attributes that do not match how you are using it, which is worse than none
genericnessNote: Unrestyled vendored blocks are the fastest route to a page that looks like every other page that pasted the same block.
